courses.name: COMP 232 · Mathematics for Computer Science
courses.description: Discrete mathematics for computer science (Rosen, 9th ed.) as taught at Concordia, Fall 2026: propositional and predicate logic, rules of inference, proof techniques, sets, functions and cardinality, elements of number theory, induction and recursion, relations, equivalence relations and partial orderings.

items.prompt: What is a **proposition**?
items.answer: A declarative statement that has exactly one truth value: true ($T$) or false ($F$).
items.explanation: Commands ("Don't do that!"), questions ("What is the time?") and open statements like $x < 4$ (no single truth value until $x$ is fixed) are not propositions. The constants $T$ and $F$ are themselves propositions.

items.prompt: Why is $x < 4$ not a proposition?
items.answer: It has no single truth value: true for some $x$, false for others. Once $x$ is given a value (or quantified) it becomes a proposition.
items.explanation: It is a propositional function $P(x)$ (§1.4). By contrast $7 < 4$ is a proposition, a false one.

items.prompt: Connective names: $p \land q$ is the {{c1::conjunction}} (and), $p \lor q$ the {{c2::disjunction}} (or), $p \oplus q$ the {{c3::exclusive or}}, $p \to q$ the {{c4::conditional (implication)}}.
items.explanation: $\neg p$ is the negation and $p \leftrightarrow q$ the biconditional ("if and only if").

items.prompt: $q$: "The student answered the question correctly." Which English sentences express $\neg q$?
items.answer: "It is not the case that the student answered the question correctly" or "The student did not answer the question correctly".
items.explanation: Not "answered incorrectly" and not "didn't answer": each of those is only one way of failing to answer correctly, so they are stronger than $\neg q$.

items.prompt: What is a truth table, and what does this course require of one used as a proof?
items.answer: A table listing every possible assignment of truth values to the propositional variables and the resulting value of the compound proposition. Used as a proof it must be complete and fully explicit: every row, every intermediate column.

items.prompt: How many rows does the truth table of a compound proposition with $n$ propositional variables have?
items.explanation: Each variable is independently $T$ or $F$. With $p, q, r$ there are $2^3 = 8$ rows; list them systematically (TTT, TTF, TFT, …) so none is missed.

items.prompt: When is $p \to q$ false?
items.answer: Only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false. In the other three rows it is true.
items.explanation: So a conditional with a false hypothesis is automatically true, and one with a true conclusion is automatically true. No causal link between $p$ and $q$ is required.

items.prompt: Truth value of $(1 + 1 = 3) \to (2 + 2 = 4)$?
items.answer: True.
items.explanation: The hypothesis $1 + 1 = 3$ is false, and a conditional with a false hypothesis is true whatever the conclusion is.

items.prompt: Is $p \lor q$ true when both $p$ and $q$ are true?
items.answer: Yes. $\lor$ is the *inclusive* or; only $p \oplus q$ (exclusive or) is false when both are true.
items.explanation: Row $T, T$: $p \lor q = T$ but $p \oplus q = F$. Everyday "or" is often exclusive ("soup or salad"); in logic always read $\lor$ inclusively.

items.prompt: $p \oplus q$ is true exactly when {{c1::exactly one of $p$, $q$ is true}}, so $p \oplus q \equiv {{c2::\neg(p \leftrightarrow q)}}$.
items.explanation: Truth-table column of $\oplus$: $F, T, T, F$, the complement of the biconditional's $T, F, F, T$.

items.prompt: $p \leftrightarrow q$ is true exactly when {{c1::$p$ and $q$ have the same truth value}}; it is read "$p$ {{c2::if and only if}} $q$".
items.explanation: Column $T, F, F, T$. "iff" abbreviates "if and only if".

items.prompt: $p \leftrightarrow q \equiv {{c1::(p \to q) \land (q \to p)}}$
items.explanation: Proved by truth table in W1 (Question 8). This is why proving an "iff" theorem takes two proofs, one per direction.

items.prompt: $p \leftrightarrow q \equiv {{c1::(p \land q) \lor (\neg p \land \neg q)}}$
items.explanation: Either both true or both false. Proved by truth table in W1 (Question 9) and reused in Question 12 to expand $q \leftrightarrow p$.

items.prompt: English forms of $p \to q$: "if $p$ then $q$", "$p$ only if $q$", "$q$ whenever $p$", "$p$ is {{c1::sufficient}} for $q$", "$q$ is {{c2::necessary}} for $p$".
items.explanation: The hypothesis is the sufficient condition and the conclusion the necessary one: $p$ being true is enough to guarantee $q$, and $q$ must hold for $p$ to hold.

items.prompt: Translate "$p$ only if $q$" into logic.
items.answer: $p \to q$
items.explanation: "Only if" points to the necessary condition: $p$ can be true only when $q$ is. The common mistake is writing $q \to p$. "You pass only if you sit the exam" means pass $\to$ sat.

items.prompt: The **converse** of $p \to q$ is ${{c1::q \to p}}$.
items.explanation: Swap hypothesis and conclusion. "If you can take COMP 238, you are a CS student" is the converse of "If you are a CS student, you can take COMP 238".

items.prompt: The **contrapositive** of $p \to q$ is ${{c1::\neg q \to \neg p}}$.
items.explanation: Swap *and* negate. "If you cannot take COMP 238, you are not a CS student."

items.prompt: The **inverse** of $p \to q$ is ${{c1::\neg p \to \neg q}}$.
items.explanation: Negate both sides without swapping. "If you are not a CS student, you cannot take COMP 238."

items.prompt: Which of the converse, inverse and contrapositive of $p \to q$ is logically equivalent to $p \to q$?
items.answer: Only the contrapositive $\neg q \to \neg p$. Neither the converse nor the inverse is equivalent to $p \to q$.
items.explanation: Row $p = F, q = T$: $p \to q$ is $T$, but the converse $q \to p$ is $F$ and the inverse $\neg p \to \neg q$ is $F$.

items.prompt: Derive $p \to q \equiv \neg q \to \neg p$ using named equivalences.
items.answer:
$p 	o q \equiv 
eg p \lor q$ (implication) $\equiv q \lor 
eg p$ (commutative) $\equiv 
eg(
eg q) \lor 
eg p$ (double negation) $\equiv 
eg q 	o 
eg p$ (implication).

items.prompt: A theorem says "if $n$ is even then $n^2$ is even". Does it tell you anything about $n$ when $n^2$ is even?
items.answer: No. That is the converse ($q \to p$), which does not follow from $p \to q$ and needs its own proof (here it happens to be true, by an indirect proof).

items.prompt: When are two compound propositions $p$ and $q$ **logically equivalent** ($p \equiv q$)?
items.answer: When they have the same truth table; equivalently, when $p \leftrightarrow q$ is a tautology.
items.explanation: Two ways to check: build both columns and compare row by row, or transform one into the other with named equivalences.

items.prompt: State the **identity laws** of propositional logic.
items.answer: $p \land T \equiv p$ and $p \lor F \equiv p$
items.explanation: $T$ is neutral for $\land$ and $F$ is neutral for $\lor$, like $1$ for $\times$ and $0$ for $+$.

items.prompt: State the **domination laws**.
items.answer: $p \lor T \equiv T$ and $p \land F \equiv F$
items.explanation: The constant wins: anything or-ed with $T$ is $T$; anything and-ed with $F$ is $F$.
items.mnemonic: Identity leaves $p$ alone; domination swallows it.

items.prompt: State the **idempotent laws**.
items.answer: $p \land p \equiv p$ and $p \lor p \equiv p$

items.prompt: State the **double negation law**.
items.answer: $\neg(\neg p) \equiv p$

items.prompt: State the **commutative laws**.
items.answer: $p \land q \equiv q \land p$ and $p \lor q \equiv q \lor p$

items.prompt: State the **associative laws**.
items.answer: $(p \land q) \land r \equiv p \land (q \land r)$ and $(p \lor q) \lor r \equiv p \lor (q \lor r)$
items.explanation: So parentheses can be dropped in a chain of one connective, but not when $\land$ and $\lor$ are mixed.

items.prompt: Distributive law: $p \land (q \lor r) \equiv {{c1::(p \land q) \lor (p \land r)}}$
items.explanation: Like multiplication over addition. Check: if $p = T$ both sides reduce to $q \lor r$; if $p = F$ both are $F$.

items.prompt: Distributive law: $p \lor (q \land r) \equiv {{c1::(p \lor q) \land (p \lor r)}}$
items.explanation: Unlike arithmetic, *both* connectives distribute over each other. Check: if $p = T$ both sides are $T$; if $p = F$ both reduce to $q \land r$.

items.prompt:
De Morgan: $
eg(p \land q) \equiv {{c1::
eg p \lor 
eg q}}$
items.explanation: "Not both" means "at least one fails". Row $p = T, q = F$: left side $\neg F = T$, right side $F \lor T = T$.

items.prompt:
De Morgan: $
eg(p \lor q) \equiv {{c1::
eg p \land 
eg q}}$
items.explanation: "Neither" means "both fail". Negation flips $\lor$ to $\land$ and negates each part.

items.prompt:
What is wrong with writing $
eg(p \land q) \equiv 
eg p \land 
eg q$?
items.answer:
The connective must flip: $
eg(p \land q) \equiv 
eg p \lor 
eg q$.
items.explanation:
Counterexample row $p = T, q = F$: $
eg(T \land F) = T$ but $
eg T \land 
eg F = F$.

items.prompt: State the **negation laws**.
items.answer: $p \lor \neg p \equiv T$ and $p \land \neg p \equiv F$
items.explanation: A proposition or its negation always holds (excluded middle), never both.

items.prompt: State the **absorption laws**.
items.answer: $p \land (p \lor q) \equiv p$ and $p \lor (p \land q) \equiv p$
items.explanation: The outer $p$ absorbs the inner term: if $p$ is true, $p \lor (p \land q)$ is true; if $p$ is false, so is $p \land q$.

items.prompt: Prove the absorption law $p \lor (p \land q) \equiv p$ with named laws.
items.answer: $p \lor (p \land q) \equiv (p \land T) \lor (p \land q)$ (identity) $\equiv p \land (T \lor q)$ (distributive) $\equiv p \land T$ (domination) $\equiv p$ (identity).

items.prompt: Implication as a disjunction: $p \to q \equiv {{c1::\neg p \lor q}}$
items.explanation: The most used equivalence: it removes $\to$ so that De Morgan and distributive laws apply. Both sides are false only in row $p = T, q = F$.

items.prompt: $\neg(p \to q) \equiv {{c1::p \land \neg q}}$
items.explanation: From $\neg(\neg p \lor q)$ by De Morgan and double negation. A conditional fails only when the hypothesis holds and the conclusion does not.

items.prompt: $p \lor q \equiv {{c1::\neg p \to q}}$
items.explanation: Apply the implication law to the right side: $\neg(\neg p) \lor q \equiv p \lor q$. Turns "it will rain or we go to the beach" into "if it does not rain, we go to the beach".

items.prompt: $(p \land q) \to r \equiv {{c1::p \to (q \to r)}}$
items.explanation:
Both sides are false only when $p, q$ are true and $r$ is false. Expand: $
eg(p \land q) \lor r \equiv 
eg p \lor 
eg q \lor r \equiv 
eg p \lor (q 	o r)$.

items.prompt: $(p \to r) \land (q \to r) \equiv {{c1::(p \lor q) \to r}}$
items.explanation:
Expand: $(
eg p \lor r) \land (
eg q \lor r) \equiv (
eg p \land 
eg q) \lor r \equiv 
eg(p \lor q) \lor r$. This is the logic behind proof by cases.

items.prompt: How do you show that two compound propositions are **not** logically equivalent?
items.answer: Give one truth-value assignment (one row) where they take different values: a counterexample.
items.explanation: One row refutes; proving an equivalence needs the whole table or an algebraic chain of named laws.

items.prompt: What must each step of an algebraic equivalence proof include in this course?
items.answer: The name of the law used (identity, De Morgan, distributive, implication, …) justifying that step.
items.explanation: W1 Question 12 is the model: every line is annotated. Typical plan: eliminate $\to$ and $\leftrightarrow$, push $\neg$ inward with De Morgan, then distribute, absorb and simplify to $T$ or $F$.

items.prompt: What is a **tautology**?
items.answer: A compound proposition that is true for every truth-value assignment to its variables.
items.explanation: Final truth-table column all $T$. Example: $p \lor \neg p$.

items.prompt: What is a **contradiction** (in the sense of §1.3)?
items.answer: A compound proposition that is false for every truth-value assignment.
items.explanation: Final column all $F$. Example: $p \land \neg p$.

items.prompt: What is a **contingency**?
items.answer: A proposition that is neither a tautology nor a contradiction: true for some assignments, false for others.
items.explanation: Examples: $p$, $p \land q$, $p \to q$.

items.prompt: $p \lor \neg p$ is a {{c1::tautology}}, $p \land \neg p$ is a {{c2::contradiction}}, and $p \land p$ ($\equiv p$) is a {{c3::contingency}}.
Let $P(x)$ denote $x^2 > x + 2$. Then $x$ is the {{c1::variable}}, $x^2 > x + 2$ is the {{c2::predicate}}, and $P$ is the {{c3::propositional function}}.
items.explanation: $P(0)$ is $0 > 2$, false; $P(5)$ is $25 > 7$, true. Once $x$ is given a value the result is a proposition.

items.prompt: What is the **universe of discourse** (domain) of a variable?
items.answer: The set of entities the variable may range over; $\forall$ and $\exists$ assert the propositional function for every / at least one element of it.
items.explanation: Always state the domain: truth values change with it. W2 p.57 lists all eight orderings of $\forall/\exists$ for $x < y$ with $x \in \mathbb{Z}$, $y \in \mathbb{Z}^+$.

items.prompt: $\forall x\,P(x)$ is true when $P(x)$ holds for {{c1::every}} element of the domain; for a finite domain $\{u_1, \dots, u_k\}$ it means ${{c2::P(u_1) \land P(u_2) \land \cdots \land P(u_k)}}$.
$\exists x\,P(x)$ is true when $P(x)$ holds for {{c1::at least one}} element of the domain; for a finite domain it means ${{c2::P(u_1) \lor P(u_2) \lor \cdots \lor P(u_k)}}$.
items.explanation: Expanding quantifiers over a small domain like $\{1, 2, 3\}$ into $\land / \lor$ chains is a standard exercise (A2).

items.prompt: Translate "All computer science students have a CS account" (domain: students; $cs(x)$, $acct(x)$).
items.answer: $\forall x\,[cs(x) \to acct(x)]$
items.explanation: Use $\to$ to restrict a universally quantified variable to part of the domain: "for every student, *if* CS *then* account".

items.prompt: Translate "Some computer science students like to dance" ($cs(s)$, $dance(s)$).
items.answer: $\exists s\,[cs(s) \land dance(s)]$
items.explanation: Use $\land$ to restrict an existentially quantified variable: there is someone with *both* properties.

items.prompt: What does $\forall s\,[cs(s) \land acct(s)]$ actually say?
items.answer: Every student *is* a CS student *and* has an account: far too strong. "All CS students have an account" is $\forall s\,[cs(s) \to acct(s)]$.

items.prompt: Why is $\exists s\,[cs(s) \to dance(s)]$ the wrong translation of "some CS students like to dance"?
items.answer: It is true as soon as *any* non-CS student exists ($cs(s)$ false makes the conditional true), so it says almost nothing. Use $\exists s\,[cs(s) \land dance(s)]$.

items.prompt: What does it take to show that $\forall x\,P(x)$ is false?
items.answer: A single counterexample: one element $c$ of the domain with $P(c)$ false.
items.explanation: $\forall y\,\forall x\,(x^2 \ge x + y)$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ is refuted by $x = 1, y = 2$: $1 \not\ge 3$.

items.prompt: What does it take to show that $\exists x\,P(x)$ is true? And to show it is false?
items.answer: True: one witness $c$ with $P(c)$ true. False: an argument that $P(x)$ fails for *every* $x$ in the domain.
items.explanation: $\exists x\,\exists y\,(x^2 \ge x + y)$ over $\mathbb{Z}^+$: take $x = 2, y = 1$.

items.prompt: $\mathbb{Z}^+ = {{c1::\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}}}$ (positive integers) and $\mathbb{N} = {{c2::\{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}}}$ (natural numbers, as defined in this course); $\mathbb{Q}$ is the set of {{c3::rational numbers}}.
items.explanation: The slides warn "watch for defs": some books start $\mathbb{N}$ at 1. $\mathbb{Z}^-$ is the negative integers, $\mathbb{R}$ the reals.

items.prompt: $\neg\,\forall x\,P(x) \equiv {{c1::\exists x\,\neg P(x)}}$
items.explanation: "Not everyone passed" = "someone failed". De Morgan's law for quantifiers: over a finite domain it is De Morgan applied to $P(u_1) \land \cdots \land P(u_k)$.

items.prompt: $\neg\,\exists x\,P(x) \equiv {{c1::\forall x\,\neg P(x)}}$
items.explanation: "Nobody passed" = "everyone failed".

items.prompt: Procedure to negate a nested quantified statement so that $\neg$ sits directly in front of the predicates?
items.answer: Move $\neg$ inward one quantifier at a time, flipping $\forall \leftrightarrow \exists$ as it passes each one, then apply De Morgan (and the implication law) to the inner formula.
items.explanation:
$
eg(\exists x\, orall z\,\exists y\,[P \land Q]) \equiv  orall x\,\exists z\, orall y\,[
eg P \lor 
eg Q]$.

items.prompt: $\neg\,\forall x\,[P(x) \to Q(x)] \equiv {{c1::\exists x\,[P(x) \land \neg Q(x)]}}$
items.explanation: Flip the quantifier, then $\neg(P \to Q) \equiv P \land \neg Q$. "Not all primes are odd" = "some prime is not odd".

items.prompt:
$
eg\,\exists x\,[P(x) \land Q(x)] \equiv  orall x\,[
eg P(x) \lor 
eg Q(x)] \equiv {{c1:: orall x\,[P(x) 	o 
eg Q(x)]}}$
items.explanation: "No professors are ignorant": it is not the case that someone is a professor and ignorant, i.e. every professor is not ignorant.

items.prompt: Negate "Nobody is right all the time" in symbols and English ($right(x,t)$: person $x$ is right at time $t$).
items.answer: $\neg\,\exists x\,\forall t\,right(x,t) \equiv \forall x\,\exists t\,\neg right(x,t)$: every person is sometimes wrong.

items.prompt: Negate $\exists x\,\forall z\,\exists y\,[P(x,y) \land Q(y,z)]$ ("some student has been to a room of every building").
items.answer: $\forall x\,\exists z\,\forall y\,[\neg P(x,y) \lor \neg Q(y,z)]$: for each student there is a building in which they have been to no room.

items.prompt: Is $\neg\,\forall x\,P(x)$ the same as $\forall x\,\neg P(x)$?
items.answer:
No. $
eg\, orall x\,P(x)$ ("not all") needs only one failure: $\exists x\,
eg P(x)$. $ orall x\,
eg P(x)$ ("none") is much stronger.
items.explanation: Over $\mathbb{Z}$ with $P(x)$: "$x$ is even": "not all integers are even" is true, "no integer is even" is false.

items.prompt: Does the order matter in $\forall x\,\exists y\,R(x,y)$ versus $\exists y\,\forall x\,R(x,y)$?
items.answer: Yes. $\exists y\,\forall x$ ("one $y$ works for all $x$") implies $\forall x\,\exists y$ ("each $x$ has its own $y$"), but not conversely.
items.explanation: $R(x,y)$: $x < y$ over $\mathbb{Z}$. $\forall x\,\exists y\,(x < y)$ is true ($y = x + 1$); $\exists y\,\forall x\,(x < y)$ is false (given $y$, take $x = y + 1$).

items.prompt: Quantifiers of the same kind commute: $\forall x\,\forall y\,P \equiv {{c1::\forall y\,\forall x\,P}}$ and $\exists x\,\exists y\,P \equiv {{c2::\exists y\,\exists x\,P}}$; mixed $\forall / \exists$ do not.
"Every student is assigned an id number" with $id(n,s)$: $\exists n\,\forall s\,id(n,s)$ or $\forall s\,\exists n\,id(n,s)$?
items.answer: $\forall s\,\exists n\,id(n,s)$. The other says a single number is everybody's id.

items.prompt: Express "every student $s$ has exactly one id number".
items.answer: $\forall s\,\exists n\,[id(n,s) \land \forall m\,(id(m,s) \to m = n)]$
items.explanation: Existence ($\exists n$) plus uniqueness (any other id $m$ of $s$ equals $n$). Putting the uniqueness clause outside the scope of $\exists n$ leaves $n$ unbound (the wrong option C in W2).

items.prompt: Express "there are at least two $x$ with property $P$".
items.answer: $\exists x\,\exists y\,[x \ne y \land P(x) \land P(y)]$
items.explanation: Without $x \ne y$ the two variables could name the same element and the statement collapses to $\exists x\,P(x)$.

items.prompt: $\forall x\,[P(x) \land Q(x)] \equiv {{c1::\forall x\,P(x) \land \forall x\,Q(x)}}$ and $\exists x\,[P(x) \lor Q(x)] \equiv {{c2::\exists x\,P(x) \lor \exists x\,Q(x)}}$
items.explanation: $\forall$ distributes over $\land$, $\exists$ over $\lor$ (think of them as big $\land$ and big $\lor$).

items.prompt: Does $\forall x\,[P(x) \lor Q(x)]$ equal $\forall x\,P(x) \lor \forall x\,Q(x)$?
items.answer: No; nor does $\exists x\,[P(x) \land Q(x)]$ equal $\exists x\,P(x) \land \exists x\,Q(x)$. Only one direction holds in each case.
items.explanation: Over $\mathbb{Z}$ with $P$ = even, $Q$ = odd: every integer is even or odd, but neither "all even" nor "all odd". Some integer is even and some is odd, but none is both.

items.prompt: Translate "There is a student in this class who has been to at least one room of every building on campus" ($P(x,y)$: $x$ has been to room $y$; $Q(y,z)$: room $y$ is in building $z$).
items.answer: $\exists x\,\forall z\,\exists y\,[P(x,y) \land Q(y,z)]$
items.explanation: Quantifier order follows the English: some student, every building, some room. Putting $\exists y$ before $\forall z$ would demand one room lying in every building.

items.prompt: An **argument** is a sequence of statements; the last is the {{c1::conclusion}} and the others are the {{c2::premises}}; the symbol $\therefore$ is read {{c3::therefore}}.
When is an argument **valid**?
items.answer: When the truth of the conclusion follows necessarily, by logical form alone, from the truth of the premises: whenever all premises are true, the conclusion must be true.

items.prompt: An argument with premises $P_1, \dots, P_n$ and conclusion $Q$ is valid iff ${{c1::(P_1 \land P_2 \land \cdots \land P_n) \to Q}}$ is a {{c2::tautology}}.
items.explanation: Turns validity into a truth-table check: in every row where all premises are true, the conclusion must be true too.

items.prompt: Can a valid argument have a false conclusion?
items.answer: Yes, if at least one premise is false. Validity is about form; it guarantees a true conclusion only when the premises are true.

items.prompt: Three ways to show that a logical argument is valid, according to the course?
items.answer: Truth tables, rules of algebra (chains of logical equivalences), and rules of inference.

items.prompt: State **modus ponens**.
items.answer: $p \to q,\; p \;\therefore\; q$
items.explanation: "If I drink coffee I feel sick; I drink coffee; therefore I feel sick." Tautology $[(p \to q) \land p] \to q$: the only row with both premises true is $p = q = T$, where $q$ holds.

items.prompt: State **modus tollens**.
items.answer: $p \to q,\; \neg q \;\therefore\; \neg p$
items.explanation: Deny the conclusion to deny the hypothesis; it is modus ponens applied to the contrapositive $\neg q \to \neg p$.

items.prompt: State **hypothetical syllogism**.
items.answer: $p \to q,\; q \to r \;\therefore\; p \to r$
items.explanation: Chaining conditionals. Tautology $[(p \to q) \land (q \to r)] \to (p \to r)$.

items.prompt: State **disjunctive syllogism**.
items.answer: $p \lor q,\; \neg p \;\therefore\; q$
items.explanation: One of two holds and it is not the first, so it is the second. Tautology $[(p \lor q) \land \neg p] \to q$.

items.prompt: State the **addition** rule.
items.answer: $p \;\therefore\; p \lor q$
items.explanation:
Weakening: you may "or" anything onto a known truth. Used in W3 to turn $
eg s$ into $
eg s \lor 
eg r$ before applying De Morgan.

items.prompt: State the **simplification** rule.
items.answer: $p \land q \;\therefore\; p$
items.explanation: From a conjunction you may keep either conjunct.

items.prompt: State the **conjunction** rule.
items.answer: $p,\; q \;\therefore\; p \land q$

items.prompt: State the **resolution** rule.
items.answer: $p \lor q,\; \neg p \lor r \;\therefore\; q \lor r$
items.explanation: The complementary pair $p, \neg p$ cancels. With $r = q$: $p \lor q,\ \neg p \lor q \therefore q$. "It rains or we go to the beach; it does not rain or we see a movie; therefore beach or movie."

items.prompt: State the **contradiction rule**.
items.answer: $\neg p \to F \;\therefore\; p$
items.explanation:
If assuming $
eg p$ leads to a contradiction, $
eg p$ is false, so $p$ is true. $(
eg p 	o F) 	o p$ is a tautology. Basis of proof by contradiction.

items.prompt: State the **proof by cases** rule.
items.answer: $p \lor q,\; p \to r,\; q \to r \;\therefore\; r$
items.explanation: Whichever case holds, $r$ follows. W3 shows $[(p \lor q) \land (p \to r) \land (q \to r)] \to r$ is a tautology by simplifying the premises to $(p \lor q) \land r$.

items.prompt: Modus ponens is the tautology $[(p \to q) \land p] \to {{c1::q}}$; modus tollens is $[(p \to q) \land \neg q] \to {{c2::\neg p}}$.
Is the argument form $p \to q,\; q \to p \;\therefore\; p \lor q$ valid?
items.answer: No: with $p = q = F$ both premises are true ($F \to F$) but $p \lor q$ is false.
items.explanation: One row where the premises hold and the conclusion fails is enough to refute validity.

items.prompt: Layout of a rules-of-inference proof expected in this course?
items.answer: Numbered steps; each line is a premise or follows from earlier numbered lines, and each is annotated with the rule or equivalence used, e.g. "modus ponens from 2 and 3".

items.prompt: What is the **converse error** (Rosen: fallacy of affirming the conclusion)?
items.answer: Arguing $p \to q,\; q \;\therefore\; p$. Invalid.
items.explanation: "If the butler did it, he has blood on his hands. He has blood on his hands. Therefore he did it." Row $p = F, q = T$: premises true, conclusion false.

items.prompt: What is the **inverse error** (Rosen: fallacy of denying the hypothesis)?
items.answer: Arguing $p \to q,\; \neg p \;\therefore\; \neg q$. Invalid.
items.explanation: "If the butler is nervous, he did it. He is not nervous. Therefore he didn't do it." Row $p = F, q = T$ again: premises true, conclusion false.

items.prompt: Modus tollens vs the inverse error: both start from $p \to q$ plus a negation. What is the difference?
items.answer:
Modus tollens negates the *conclusion* ($
eg q 	herefore 
eg p$): valid. The inverse error negates the *hypothesis* ($
eg p 	herefore 
eg q$): invalid.

items.prompt: Modus ponens vs the converse error?
items.answer: Modus ponens affirms the *hypothesis* ($p \therefore q$): valid. The converse error affirms the *conclusion* ($q \therefore p$): invalid.
items.explanation: Both fallacies amount to using $q \to p$ or $\neg p \to \neg q$, neither of which is equivalent to $p \to q$.

items.prompt: State **universal instantiation**.
items.answer: $\forall x\,P(x) \;\therefore\; P(c)$ for any particular $c$ in the domain.
items.explanation: "All men are mortal, so Socrates is mortal" needs UI first, then modus ponens.

items.prompt: State **universal generalization**.
items.answer: $P(c)$ for an *arbitrary* $c$ in the domain $\;\therefore\; \forall x\,P(x)$
items.explanation: Allowed only when nothing was assumed about $c$ beyond being in the domain (no undischarged assumption restricts $c$). This is how "let $x$ be arbitrary … hence for all $x$" proofs end.

items.prompt: State **existential instantiation**.
items.answer: $\exists x\,P(x) \;\therefore\; P(c)$ for some element $c$.
items.explanation: $c$ must be a *fresh* name for the unknown witness, not an arbitrary element and not a name already in use.

items.prompt: State **existential generalization**.
items.answer: $P(c)$ for some particular $c$ in the domain $\;\therefore\; \exists x\,P(x)$
items.explanation: Exhibiting one witness proves existence.

items.prompt: State **universal modus ponens**.
items.answer: $\forall x\,(P(x) \to Q(x)),\; P(c) \;\therefore\; Q(c)$
items.explanation: Universal instantiation followed by modus ponens, packaged as one rule.

items.prompt: State **universal modus tollens**.
items.answer: $\forall x\,(P(x) \to Q(x)),\; \neg Q(c) \;\therefore\; \neg P(c)$
items.explanation: Universal instantiation followed by modus tollens.

items.prompt: Formal steps proving "Socrates is mortal" from "all men are mortal" and "Socrates is a man" ($N$: man, $M$: mortal).
items.answer: 1. $\forall x\,(N(x) \to M(x))$, premise. 2. $N(S) \to M(S)$, universal instantiation from 1. 3. $N(S)$, premise. 4. $M(S)$, modus ponens from 2 and 3.

items.prompt: Why can't you conclude $\forall x\,P(x)$ from $\exists x\,P(x)$ by existential instantiation followed by universal generalization?
items.answer: EI gives $P(c)$ for a *specific* unknown witness $c$, not an arbitrary one; UG requires $c$ to be arbitrary.

items.prompt: When a derivation uses both existential and universal instantiation, which goes first and why?
items.answer: EI first: it names a new witness $c$; then UI can instantiate the universal premises at that same $c$. In the other order the universal $c$ would have to coincide with the witness, which EI cannot guarantee.
items.explanation: Lewis Carroll style: from $\exists x\,(L(x) \land \neg C(x))$ get $L(c) \land \neg C(c)$ first, then instantiate $\forall x\,(L(x) \to F(x))$ at $c$.

items.prompt: What is a **theorem**?
items.answer: A statement that can be proved to be true.
items.explanation: $(p \to q) \leftrightarrow (\neg p \lor q)$ is a theorem (shown by truth table). "There is life on Europa" is an empirical claim, not a theorem.

items.prompt: What is a **proof** of a statement $s$?
items.answer: A finite sequence of statements $s_1, \dots, s_n = s$ in which each $s_i$ is an axiom, a definition, an assumption (hypothesis) of the theorem, a previously proven theorem, or follows from earlier statements by a rule of inference.

items.prompt: What is an **axiom**?
items.answer: A statement accepted as true without proof.
items.explanation: Geometry: exactly one straight line through two distinct points. Classical logic: every proposition is either true or false, not both.

items.prompt: $m$ is **even** $\iff \exists i \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $m = {{c1::2i}}$; $m$ is **odd** $\iff \exists i \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $m = {{c2::2i + 1}}$.
items.explanation: Every parity proof starts by unpacking this definition and ends by repacking it: show $n^2 = 2j$ for some integer $j$.

items.prompt: A real number is **rational** iff it equals ${{c1::a / b}}$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$, $b \ne 0$; otherwise it is {{c2::irrational}}.
items.explanation: In contradiction proofs you may also assume the fraction is in lowest terms (no common factor greater than 1).

items.prompt: Proof methods named in COMP 232: direct proof, {{c1::indirect proof}} (via the contrapositive), {{c2::proof by contradiction}}, {{c3::proof by cases}}, and mathematical induction.
Template of a **direct proof** of $p \to q$?
items.answer: Assume $p$ is true; derive a chain $p \to q_1 \to \cdots \to q_n \to q$ using definitions, axioms, known theorems and rules of inference; conclude $q$.

items.prompt: What is an **indirect proof** of $p \to q$ in this course?
items.answer:
A direct proof of the contrapositive $
eg q 	o 
eg p$: assume $
eg q$ and derive $
eg p$. Justified by $p 	o q \equiv 
eg q 	o 
eg p$.
items.explanation: Rosen calls this "proof by contraposition". Do not confuse it with proof by contradiction, which assumes $p \land \neg q$ and derives $F$.

items.prompt: Template of a **proof by contradiction** of a statement $p$?
items.answer: Assume $\neg p$ and derive a contradiction ($F$); by the contradiction rule $\neg p \to F \;\therefore\; p$, the statement $p$ holds.
items.explanation: Also called *reductio ad absurdum*. Used for "$\sqrt{2}$ is irrational" and "there are infinitely many primes".

items.prompt: To prove $p \to q$ by contradiction, assume ${{c1::p \land \neg q}}$ and derive $F$; this works because $(p \land \neg q) \to F \equiv {{c2::p \to q}}$.
items.explanation:
$(p \land 
eg q) 	o F \equiv 
eg(p \land 
eg q) \lor F \equiv 
eg p \lor q \equiv p 	o q$.

items.prompt: Template of a **proof by cases** for $(A_1 \lor A_2 \lor \cdots \lor A_n) \to C$?
items.answer: Prove each $A_i \to C$ separately; then $C$ holds whenever some $A_i$ does. The cases must cover every possibility.
items.explanation: Typical case splits: $x \ge y$ vs $x < y$; $n$ even vs odd; $n \bmod 3 \in \{0, 1, 2\}$; the remainders of the division algorithm.

items.prompt: How do you prove $p \leftrightarrow q$?
items.answer: Usually with two proofs: $p \to q$ and $q \to p$, possibly by different methods.
items.explanation: "$n$ is even $\iff n^2$ is even": direct proof forwards, indirect proof backwards.

items.prompt: Direct proof that if $n$ is even then $n^2$ is even.
items.answer: $n = 2i$ for some integer $i$, so $n^2 = 4i^2 = 2(2i^2)$; since $2i^2$ is an integer, $n^2$ is even by definition.

items.prompt: Prove: if $n^2$ is even then $n$ is even.
items.answer: Indirect proof (contrapositive): if $n$ is odd then $n^2$ is odd. $n = 2i + 1 \Rightarrow n^2 = 4i^2 + 4i + 1 = 2(2i^2 + 2i) + 1$, which is odd.
items.explanation: Starting from "$n^2$ even" gives nothing usable about $n$; "$n$ odd" gives a formula to square. That is the signal for an indirect proof.

items.prompt: Prove by contradiction: if $3n + 2$ is odd then $n$ is odd.
items.answer: Assume $3n + 2$ is odd and $n$ is even, $n = 2k$. Then $3n + 2 = 6k + 2 = 2(3k + 1)$ is even, contradicting the assumption. So $n$ is odd.

items.prompt: Prove $\max\{x, y\} + \min\{x, y\} = x + y$ for all reals $x, y$.
items.answer: Cases. If $x \ge y$: $\max = x$, $\min = y$, sum $x + y$. If $x < y$: $\max = y$, $\min = x$, sum $y + x = x + y$. These two cases are exhaustive.

items.prompt: Show that the square of any integer has the form $4k$ or $4k + 1$.
items.explanation: Proof by cases on the remainder; each case names the integer $k$ explicitly.

items.prompt: What is a **vacuous proof** of $p \to q$?
items.answer: Show that the hypothesis $p$ is false; then $p \to q$ is true regardless of $q$.
items.explanation: "If $0 > 1$ then …" is true. This is also why $\forall x\,P(x)$ holds over an empty domain and why $\emptyset \subseteq A$.

items.prompt: What is a **trivial proof** of $p \to q$, and how does it differ from a vacuous proof?
items.answer: Show that the conclusion $q$ is true (whatever $p$ is). Vacuous: hypothesis false; trivial: conclusion true.

items.prompt: How do you disprove a universal claim (a conjecture of the form $\forall x\,P(x)$)?
items.answer: With one counterexample.
items.explanation: Euler's conjecture that $a^4 + b^4 + c^4 = d^4$ has no positive integer solutions fell to a single counterexample: $a = 95800, b = 217519, c = 414560, d = 422481$.

items.prompt: What is wrong with a proof of $p \to q$ that starts by assuming $q$?
items.answer: It is circular (begs the question): it uses what is to be proved. Likewise, deriving $p$ from $q$ proves the converse, not $p \to q$.

items.prompt: Outline the proof that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
items.answer: Assume $\sqrt{2} = a/b$ in lowest terms. Then $2b^2 = a^2$, so $a^2$ is even, so $a$ is even, $a = 2i$. Then $b^2 = 2i^2$, so $b$ is even. Both even contradicts lowest terms.
items.explanation: Proof by contradiction: assume the negation ("rational") and derive $F$. The step "$a^2$ even $\Rightarrow a$ even" is the indirect-proof lemma from Example 2, used twice.

items.prompt: Outline Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes.
items.answer: Assume finitely many primes $p_1, \dots, p_n$. Let $N = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n + 1$. Since $N > p_n$, some $p_i$ must divide $N$; but $N \bmod p_i = 1$ for every $i$. Contradiction.

items.prompt: In Euclid's proof, is $N = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n + 1$ claimed to be prime?
items.answer: No. The contradiction is only that no listed prime divides $N$, although every integer larger than $p_n$ would have to have a prime divisor from the list.
items.explanation: $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 \cdot 509$ is not prime.

items.prompt: Prove there is no integer $n > 3$ with $n$, $n + 2$ and $n + 4$ all prime.
items.answer: Cases on $n \bmod 3$: if $0$, $3 \mid n$; if $1$, $3 \mid n + 2$; if $2$, $3 \mid n + 4$. The divisible number exceeds 3, so it is not prime: a contradiction in every case.

items.prompt: What is **backward reasoning** as a proof strategy?
items.answer: If you cannot prove $p$ directly, find a statement $q$ such that $q \to p$ is known and $q$ is easier; then prove $q$.

items.prompt: Element-wise proof that $A \subseteq A \cup B$.
items.answer: Let $x$ be arbitrary with $x \in A$. Then $x \in A \lor x \in B$ (addition), so $x \in A \cup B$ by definition of union. Since $x$ was arbitrary, $A \subseteq A \cup B$ (universal generalization).

items.prompt: What is a set, and what are the three ways of specifying one given in the slides?
items.answer: A collection of objects (its members or elements). Specify it by listing the elements in braces, $\{0, 1\}$; by listing with a pattern, $\{\dots, -1, 0, 1, \dots\}$; or by set-builder notation $\{x \mid P(x)\}$.
items.explanation: $\{x \mid P(x)\}$ reads "the set of all $x$ such that $P(x)$"; the slides also write $\{x : P(x)\}$.

items.prompt: $A \subseteq B \iff {{c1::\forall x\,(x \in A \to x \in B)}}$
items.explanation: To prove $A \subseteq B$: take an arbitrary $x \in A$ and show $x \in B$.

items.prompt: $A = B \iff {{c1::(A \subseteq B) \land (B \subseteq A)}}$
items.explanation: Double inclusion: the standard way to prove two sets equal when no identity applies directly.

items.prompt: $A \subset B$ (proper subset) $\iff {{c1::(A \subseteq B) \land (A \ne B)}}$
items.explanation: The course writes $\subset$ for proper subset; $\subseteq$ allows equality.

items.prompt: Is $\emptyset \subseteq A$ for every set $A$?
items.answer: Yes, vacuously: $\forall x\,(x \in \emptyset \to x \in A)$ holds because $x \in \emptyset$ is always false.

items.prompt: For $A = \{1, 2\}$, which are true: $1 \in A$, $\{1\} \in A$, $\{1\} \subseteq A$, $1 \subseteq A$?
items.answer: $1 \in A$ and $\{1\} \subseteq A$ are true. $\{1\} \in A$ is false (the object $\{1\}$ is not listed in $A$), and $1 \subseteq A$ is meaningless since $1$ is not a set.
items.explanation: $\in$ relates an element to a set; $\subseteq$ relates two sets.

items.prompt: Compare $\emptyset$ and $\{\emptyset\}$: cardinalities, and are $\emptyset \in \{\emptyset\}$ and $\emptyset \subseteq \{\emptyset\}$ true?
items.answer: $|\emptyset| = 0$ and $|\{\emptyset\}| = 1$. Both $\emptyset \in \{\emptyset\}$ and $\emptyset \subseteq \{\emptyset\}$ are true.

items.prompt: Define the **cardinality** of a finite set.
items.answer: If $A$ has exactly $k$ distinct elements for some natural number $k$, $A$ is finite and its cardinality is $|A| = k$. Otherwise $A$ is infinite.
items.explanation: $\{i \in \mathbb{Z} : 1 \le i \le 26\}$ has cardinality 26; the set of primes is infinite.

items.prompt: $A \cup B = \{x \mid {{c1::(x \in A) \lor (x \in B)}}\}$
$A \cap B = \{x \mid {{c1::(x \in A) \land (x \in B)}}\}$
$A - B = \{x \mid {{c1::(x \in A) \land (x \notin B)}}\}$
items.explanation: The elements of $A$ that are not in $B$. Not symmetric: $A - B = B - A$ forces $A = B$.

items.prompt: $\overline{A} = {{c1::U - A}} = \{x \mid x \notin A\}$
items.explanation: Depends on the universal set $U$ in force.

items.prompt: Define the **power set** $\mathcal{P}(A)$ and write out $\mathcal{P}(\{1, 2, 3\})$.
items.explanation: Always includes $\emptyset$ and $A$ itself.

items.prompt: If $|A| = n$ then $|\mathcal{P}(A)| = {{c1::2^n}}$.
items.explanation: Each element is in or out of a subset: $n$ independent binary choices. Matches the bit-string representation of subsets.

items.prompt: What is $\mathcal{P}(\emptyset)$?
items.answer: $\{\emptyset\}$, a one-element set (not $\emptyset$).
items.explanation: The empty set has exactly one subset: itself. $|\mathcal{P}(\emptyset)| = 2^0 = 1$.

items.prompt: $A \times B = \{{{c1::(a, b) \mid a \in A \text{ and } b \in B}}\}$, the set of ordered pairs; $|A \times B| = {{c2::|A| \cdot |B|}}$.
items.explanation: $\{1, 2\} \times \{x, y, z\}$ has 6 pairs; $(1, x) \in A \times B$ but $(x, 1) \notin A \times B$, since order matters.

items.prompt: $A$ and $B$ are **disjoint** iff ${{c1::A \cap B = \emptyset}}$; $A_1, \dots, A_n$ are **pairwise (mutually) disjoint** iff ${{c2::A_i \cap A_j = \emptyset}}$ whenever $i \ne j$.
items.explanation: Pairwise disjoint is stronger than $A_1 \cap \cdots \cap A_n = \emptyset$: three sets can have empty triple intersection while two of them overlap.

items.prompt: When is $\{A_1, \dots, A_n\}$ a **partition** of $A$?
items.answer: When the $A_i$ are non-empty, $A = A_1 \cup \cdots \cup A_n$, and the $A_i$ are pairwise disjoint.
items.explanation: Every element of $A$ lies in exactly one block. Equivalence classes (§9.5) always form a partition.

items.prompt: State the set **identity laws**.
items.answer: $A \cup \emptyset = A$ and $A \cap U = A$
items.explanation: Mirror of $p \lor F \equiv p$ and $p \land T \equiv p$.

items.prompt: State the set **domination laws**.
items.answer: $A \cup U = U$ and $A \cap \emptyset = \emptyset$

items.prompt: State the **complement law** of the course's identity table (Rosen: complementation law).
items.answer: $\overline{\overline{A}} = A$
items.explanation: Double complement, the mirror of double negation. The slides label this row simply "complement".

items.prompt: State the set **commutative laws**.
items.answer: $A \cup B = B \cup A$ and $A \cap B = B \cap A$

items.prompt: State the set **associative laws**.
items.answer: $(A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)$ and $(A \cap B) \cap C = A \cap (B \cap C)$

items.prompt: Distributive law: $A \cup (B \cap C) = {{c1::(A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)}}$
Distributive law: $A \cap (B \cup C) = {{c1::(A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)}}$
De Morgan: $\overline{A \cap B} = {{c1::\overline{A} \cup \overline{B}}}$
items.explanation:
Not in both = missing from at least one. Element proof: $
eg(x \in A \land x \in B) \equiv x 
otin A \lor x 
otin B$.

items.prompt: De Morgan: $\overline{A \cup B} = {{c1::\overline{A} \cap \overline{B}}}$
items.explanation: In neither = outside both.

items.prompt: State the two "other useful identities" for a set and its complement (Rosen: complement laws).
items.answer: $A \cup \overline{A} = U$ and $A \cap \overline{A} = \emptyset$
items.explanation: Mirror of the negation laws $p \lor \neg p \equiv T$ and $p \land \neg p \equiv F$. The slides list them unnamed on the "Other useful identities" page.

items.prompt: $A - B = {{c1::A \cap \overline{B}}}$
items.explanation: The first move in almost every algebraic set proof: rewrite differences as intersections with complements.

items.prompt: $A \cap B \subseteq {{c1::A}}$, $A \subseteq {{c2::A \cup B}}$, and $(A \subseteq B) \land (B \subseteq C) \Rightarrow {{c3::A \subseteq C}}$ (transitivity).
If $A \cup B = A$ then ${{c1::B \subseteq A}}$; if $A \cap B = A$ then ${{c2::A \subseteq B}}$.
items.explanation: Union absorbs the smaller set; intersection returns the smaller set.

items.prompt: If $A - B = A$ then ${{c1::A \cap B = \emptyset}}$; if $A - B = B - A$ then ${{c2::A = B}}$.
items.explanation: Second: an $x \in A - B$ would have to lie in $B - A$ too, impossible; so $A - B = \emptyset$ and symmetrically $B - A = \emptyset$.

items.prompt: Set-to-logic dictionary: $\cup$ corresponds to ${{c1::\lor}}$, $\cap$ to ${{c2::\land}}$, complement to ${{c3::\neg}}$, and $\subseteq$ to ${{c4::\to}}$.
items.explanation: Every logical equivalence has a set-identity twin, which is why element proofs reduce to propositional logic.

items.prompt: Three ways to prove a set identity in this course?
items.answer: An element proof (set-builder notation plus logical equivalences), an algebraic proof (chain of set identities), or a membership table.

items.prompt: Element proof that $A \cup (B - A) = A \cup B$ (key steps).
items.answer: $\{x : x \in A \lor (x \in B \land x \notin A)\} = \{x : (x \in A \lor x \in B) \land (x \in A \lor x \notin A)\}$ (distributive) $= \{x : (x \in A \lor x \in B) \land T\} = \{x : x \in A \cup B\}$.

items.prompt: Algebraic proof that $A \cup (B - A) = A \cup B$.
items.answer: $A \cup (B - A) = A \cup (B \cap \overline{A}) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup \overline{A})$ (distributive) $= (A \cup B) \cap U$ (complement law) $= A \cup B$ (identity law).

items.prompt: With $U = \{a_1, \dots, a_k\}$ in a fixed order, a subset is stored as a bit string of length $k$ whose $i$-th bit is 1 iff $a_i$ is in it; then $\cap$ is bitwise {{c1::AND}}, $\cup$ bitwise {{c2::OR}}, complement bitwise {{c3::NOT}}.
items.explanation: $U = \{a, e, i, o, u\}$: $01101$ is $\{e, i, u\}$, $11111$ is $U$, $00000$ is $\emptyset$. Bitwise operations on words are fast, which is why sets are stored this way.

items.prompt: $(A \cup B) - C = {{c1::(A - C) \cup (B - C)}}$ and $A - (B \cup C) = {{c2::(A - B) - C}}$
items.explanation: Both follow by rewriting $- C$ as $\cap\, \overline{C}$ and using the distributive, De Morgan and associative laws.

items.prompt: A function $f : A \to B$ assigns to each element of $A$ {{c1::exactly one}} element of $B$; $A$ is the {{c2::domain}} and $B$ the {{c3::codomain}}.
items.explanation: The range (image) $f(A) = \{f(a) : a \in A\}$ is the set of values actually taken; it is a subset of the codomain.

items.prompt: Range vs codomain of $f : A \to B$?
items.answer: The codomain $B$ is the declared target set; the range $f(A)$ is the set of values actually attained. $f$ is onto iff range $=$ codomain.
items.explanation: $f(x) = x^2$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$: codomain $\mathbb{R}$, range $[0, \infty)$.

items.prompt: $\lfloor x \rfloor$ is the largest integer {{c1::$\le x$}} and $\lceil x \rceil$ the smallest integer {{c2::$\ge x$}}; so $\lfloor -1.5 \rfloor = {{c3::-2}}$.
items.explanation: Common error: $\lfloor -1.5 \rfloor = -1$. Floor goes *down* on the number line, also for negatives; $\lceil -1.5 \rceil = -1$.

items.prompt: Define $(f \circ g)(x)$. Which function is applied first?
items.answer: $(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$: apply $g$ first, then $f$. It requires the range of $g$ to lie in the domain of $f$.
items.explanation: Read right to left. In general $f \circ g \ne g \circ f$.

items.prompt: $f$ is **one-to-one (injective)** iff ${{c1::f(a) = f(b) \to a = b}}$ for all $a, b$ in the domain.
items.explanation: Equivalently $a \ne b \to f(a) \ne f(b)$, the form used in W4 Example 7. Distinct inputs give distinct outputs.

items.prompt: $f : A \to B$ is **onto (surjective)** iff ${{c1::\forall b \in B\;\exists a \in A\; f(a) = b}}$.
items.explanation: Every element of the codomain is hit by some element of the domain.

items.prompt: $f$ is a **bijection** (one-to-one correspondence) iff it is both {{c1::one-to-one and onto}}; exactly then $f$ has an {{c2::inverse}} $f^{-1} : B \to A$ with $f^{-1}(b) = a \iff f(a) = b$.
How do you prove, or disprove, that $f$ is one-to-one?
items.answer:
Prove: assume $f(a) = f(b)$ and deduce $a = b$ (or show $a 
e b \Rightarrow f(a) 
e f(b)$, splitting into cases if $f$ is piecewise). Disprove: exhibit $a 
e b$ with $f(a) = f(b)$.
items.explanation: W4 Example 7 handles $f(n) = n + 1$ ($n$ even), $n - 3$ ($n$ odd) by cases on the parities of $m$ and $n$.

items.prompt: How do you prove, or disprove, that $f : A \to B$ is onto?
items.answer: Prove: take an arbitrary $b \in B$ and produce $a \in A$ with $f(a) = b$ (solve for $a$ and check it lies in $A$). Disprove: exhibit one $b$ with no preimage.

items.prompt: Is $f(x) = x^2$ from $\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ one-to-one? Onto?
items.answer: Neither: $f(-1) = f(1)$ breaks one-to-one, and $-1$ has no preimage so it is not onto. Domain and codomain matter: as a map from $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ to $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ it is a bijection.

items.prompt: When do two sets $A$ and $B$ (possibly infinite) have the same cardinality, $|A| = |B|$?
items.answer: When there is a bijection (one-to-one correspondence) between them. $|A| \le |B|$ means there is a one-to-one function from $A$ to $B$.

items.prompt: A set is **countable** iff it is finite or has the same cardinality as {{c1::$\mathbb{Z}^+$}} (countably infinite, cardinality $\aleph_0$); to show it, exhibit an {{c2::enumeration $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$}} that lists every element.
items.explanation: $\mathbb{Z}$: $0, 1, -1, 2, -2, \dots$ The positive rationals: snake through the grid of fractions $p/q$, skipping repeats.

items.prompt: Why is the set of real numbers in $(0, 1)$ uncountable?
items.answer: Cantor's diagonal argument: given any list $r_1, r_2, \dots$ of decimals, build a number whose $i$-th digit differs from the $i$-th digit of $r_i$ (and avoids 0 and 9). It lies in $(0,1)$ but is not on the list, so no list is complete.

items.prompt: For integers $a \ne 0$ and $b$, $a \mid b$ ("$a$ divides $b$") means ${{c1::\exists c \in \mathbb{Z}\; b = ac}}$.
items.explanation: $3 \mid 12$, $3 \nmid 7$. $a \mid b$ is a proposition; $a / b$ is a number. Every nonzero $a$ divides $0$.

items.prompt: If $a \mid b$ and $a \mid c$ then $a \mid {{c1::b + c}}$; if $a \mid b$ then $a \mid {{c2::bc}}$ for every integer $c$; if $a \mid b$ and $b \mid c$ then ${{c3::a \mid c}}$.
items.explanation: Together: $a \mid b$ and $a \mid c$ give $a \mid (mb + nc)$. Proof of the first: $b = ak$, $c = al$ so $b + c = a(k + l)$.

items.prompt: Division algorithm: for $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $d \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ there are unique integers $q, r$ with $a = {{c1::dq + r}}$ and ${{c2::0 \le r < d}}$; $q = a \textbf{ div } d$ and $r = a \bmod d$.
items.explanation: Basis of proofs by cases on remainders: W4 Example 9 uses $d = 4$, Example 11 uses $n \bmod 3$.

items.prompt: $-11 \textbf{ div } 3$ and $-11 \bmod 3$?
items.answer: $q = -4$ and $r = 1$, because $-11 = 3 \cdot (-4) + 1$ with $0 \le 1 < 3$.
items.explanation: The remainder is never negative: $-11 = 3 \cdot (-3) - 2$ is *not* the division-algorithm form.

items.prompt: $a \equiv b \pmod m$ iff ${{c1::m \mid (a - b)}}$; equivalently $a \bmod m = {{c2::b \bmod m}}$, or $a = b + km$ for some $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.
items.explanation: $17 \equiv 5 \pmod{6}$ since $6 \mid 12$. Note $a \bmod m$ is a number, $a \equiv b \pmod m$ a proposition.

items.prompt: If $a \equiv b \pmod m$ and $c \equiv d \pmod m$ then $a + c \equiv {{c1::b + d}} \pmod m$ and $ac \equiv {{c2::bd}} \pmod m$.
items.explanation: Proof: $a = b + sm$, $c = d + tm$, so $ac = bd + m(bt + ds + stm)$.

items.prompt: Can you cancel a common factor in a congruence: $ac \equiv bc \pmod m \Rightarrow a \equiv b \pmod m$?
items.answer: Not in general: $2 \cdot 3 \equiv 2 \cdot 0 \pmod 6$ but $3 \not\equiv 0 \pmod 6$. Cancelling $c$ is valid when $\gcd(c, m) = 1$.

items.prompt: Define prime and composite. Is $1$ prime?
items.answer: An integer $p > 1$ is prime if its only positive divisors are $1$ and $p$; an integer $> 1$ that is not prime is composite. $1$ is neither.

items.prompt: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every integer $n > 1$ can be written {{c1::uniquely}} as a product of primes (in non-decreasing order).
items.explanation: Existence is proved by strong induction; uniqueness uses: if a prime $p$ divides $ab$ then $p \mid a$ or $p \mid b$.

items.prompt: If $n$ is composite, then $n$ has a prime divisor $\le {{c1::\sqrt{n}}}$.
items.explanation: If $n = ab$ with $1 < a \le b$ then $a \le \sqrt{n}$. Contrapositive gives the primality test: if no prime $\le \sqrt n$ divides $n$, then $n$ is prime. For $101$ check only $2, 3, 5, 7$.

items.prompt: $\gcd(a, b)$ is the largest integer dividing both $a$ and $b$; $a$ and $b$ are **relatively prime** iff $\gcd(a, b) = {{c1::1}}$.
items.explanation: $a_1, \dots, a_n$ are pairwise relatively prime when every pair has gcd 1. $\gcd(0, b) = b$ for $b > 0$.

items.prompt: From prime factorizations, $\gcd$ takes the {{c1::minimum}} exponent of each prime and $\operatorname{lcm}$ the {{c2::maximum}}; hence $ab = {{c3::\gcd(a,b) \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(a,b)}}$.
items.explanation: $\min(e, f) + \max(e, f) = e + f$ for every prime exponent pair. Example: $\gcd(12, 18) = 6$, $\operatorname{lcm} = 36$, $6 \cdot 36 = 216 = 12 \cdot 18$.

items.prompt: Euclidean algorithm: $\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, {{c1::a \bmod b}})$ for $b > 0$; repeat until the remainder is $0$, and the gcd is the last {{c2::non-zero remainder}}.
items.explanation: Lemma: if $a = bq + r$ then $\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, r)$, because any common divisor of $a$ and $b$ divides $r = a - bq$, and vice versa.

items.prompt: Compute $\gcd(662, 414)$ with the Euclidean algorithm.
Mathematical induction: to prove $\forall n \ge 1\; P(n)$, show the **basis step** ${{c1::P(1)}}$ and the **inductive step** ${{c2::\forall k \ge 1\,[P(k) \to P(k+1)]}}$.
items.explanation: As a rule of inference: $[P(1) \land \forall k\,(P(k) \to P(k+1))] \to \forall n\,P(n)$. The basis may be any integer $b$; then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \ge b$.

items.prompt: What must the inductive step contain, as written in a proof?
items.answer: State the inductive hypothesis "assume $P(k)$ for an arbitrary $k \ge b$"; show $P(k+1)$, pointing out where $P(k)$ is used; conclude "by induction, $P(n)$ holds for all $n \ge b$".

items.prompt: Two common errors in induction proofs?
items.answer: Omitting the basis step (the inductive step alone proves nothing); and assuming $P(k+1)$, or $P(n)$ for all $n$, instead of $P(k)$, which is circular.

items.prompt: Inductive step for $1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.
items.answer: Assume $1 + \cdots + k = \frac{k(k+1)}{2}$. Then $1 + \cdots + k + (k+1) = \frac{k(k+1)}{2} + (k+1) = \frac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}$, which is $P(k+1)$.
items.explanation: Factor out $(k+1)$: $(k+1)\left(\frac{k}{2} + 1\right) = \frac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}$.

items.prompt: To prove $2^n < n!$ by induction, where does the basis step start, and what is the inductive step?
items.answer: Basis at $n = 4$ ($16 < 24$), since the claim fails for $n \le 3$. Step: $2^{k+1} = 2 \cdot 2^k < 2 \cdot k! \le (k+1) \cdot k! = (k+1)!$ for $k \ge 4$.

items.prompt: Strong induction: the inductive step assumes ${{c1::P(1) \land P(2) \land \cdots \land P(k)}}$ and proves $P(k+1)$.
items.explanation: Use it when $P(k+1)$ depends on a case smaller than $k$: "every $n \ge 2$ is a product of primes" splits $n = ab$ with $a, b < n$.

items.prompt: State the **well-ordering property**.
items.answer: Every non-empty set of positive integers (or of non-negative integers) has a least element.
items.explanation: Equivalent to induction. Typical use: suppose a counterexample exists, take the smallest, and derive a smaller one, a contradiction.

items.prompt: When is strong induction needed rather than ordinary induction?
items.answer: When the inductive step for $P(k+1)$ uses $P(j)$ for some $j < k$, not only $P(k)$: recurrences like $f_n = f_{n-1} + f_{n-2}$, or splitting $n$ into two smaller parts (factorization, postage with 4- and 5-cent stamps).

items.prompt: A recursive definition of a function on $\mathbb{N}$ has a {{c1::basis step}} giving $f(0)$ and a {{c2::recursive step}} giving $f(n+1)$ in terms of $f(n)$ (or earlier values).
items.explanation: Factorial: $0! = 1$ and $(n+1)! = (n+1) \cdot n!$.
$0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, \dots$ Properties are proved by strong induction with two base cases.

items.prompt: What is **structural induction**?
items.answer: To prove $P$ for every element of a recursively defined set: show $P$ holds for each basis element, and show each recursive rule preserves $P$ (if it holds for the inputs, it holds for the element built from them).
items.explanation: Strings over $\Sigma$: basis $\lambda$ (empty string); rule: $w \in \Sigma^*$, $x \in \Sigma \Rightarrow wx \in \Sigma^*$. Proof of $l(xy) = l(x) + l(y)$ goes by structural induction on $y$.

items.prompt: A binary relation from $A$ to $B$ is a {{c1::subset of $A \times B$}}; a relation on $A$ is a subset of $A \times A$; $a\,R\,b$ means ${{c2::(a, b) \in R}}$.
items.explanation: A function is a special relation in which each $a$ is paired with exactly one $b$.

items.prompt: The number of relations on a set with $n$ elements is ${{c1::2^{n^2}}}$.
items.explanation: $|A \times A| = n^2$ ordered pairs, each in or out of $R$: the power set of $A \times A$.

items.prompt: $R$ on $A$ is **reflexive** iff ${{c1::\forall a \in A\;(a, a) \in R}}$ and **symmetric** iff ${{c2::\forall a, b\;[(a, b) \in R \to (b, a) \in R]}}$.
$R$ is **antisymmetric** iff ${{c1::(a, b) \in R \land (b, a) \in R \to a = b}}$ and **transitive** iff ${{c2::(a, b) \in R \land (b, c) \in R \to (a, c) \in R}}$.
Are symmetric and antisymmetric opposites?
items.answer: No. The equality relation $\{(a, a)\}$ is both; $\{(1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 3)\}$ is neither. Antisymmetric forbids $a \ne b$ with both $(a, b)$ and $(b, a)$; symmetric demands the reverse pair.

items.prompt: Which of reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive hold for $\le$ on $\mathbb{Z}$? For $<$?
items.answer: $\le$: reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive, not symmetric. $<$: antisymmetric (vacuously) and transitive, neither reflexive nor symmetric.
items.explanation: "Divides" on $\mathbb{Z}^+$ behaves like $\le$: reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive.

items.prompt: Zero-one matrix $M_R$: $R$ is reflexive iff {{c1::every diagonal entry is 1}}, and symmetric iff ${{c2::M_R = M_R^{T}}}$.
items.explanation: $m_{ij} = 1$ iff $(a_i, a_j) \in R$. Antisymmetric: for $i \ne j$, $m_{ij} = 1$ implies $m_{ji} = 0$.

items.prompt: How are $M_{R \cup S}$, $M_{R \cap S}$ and $M_{S \circ R}$ obtained from $M_R$ and $M_S$?
items.answer: Entry-wise OR (join $\lor$) for union, entry-wise AND (meet $\land$) for intersection, and the Boolean product $M_R \odot M_S$ for the composite $S \circ R$.

items.prompt: In the digraph of $R$: reflexive iff {{c1::every vertex has a loop}}; symmetric iff {{c2::every edge has its reverse edge}}; transitive iff whenever edges $a \to b$ and $b \to c$ exist, so does $a \to c$.
What is the **closure** of a relation $R$ with respect to a property $P$?
items.answer: The smallest relation containing $R$ that has property $P$: $R \subseteq S$, $S$ has $P$, and $S \subseteq S'$ for every relation $S' \supseteq R$ with $P$.

items.prompt: Reflexive closure of $R$ on $A$: ${{c1::R \cup \Delta}}$ where $\Delta = \{(a, a) : a \in A\}$; symmetric closure: ${{c2::R \cup R^{-1}}}$ where $R^{-1} = \{(b, a) : (a, b) \in R\}$.

Transitive closure $R^{*} = {{c1::R \cup R^2 \cup R^3 \cup \cdots}}$ (the connectivity relation): $(a, b) \in R^{*}$ iff there is a {{c2::path of length $\ge 1$}} from $a$ to $b$ in the digraph of $R$.
items.explanation: On an $n$-element set only $R \cup R^2 \cup \cdots \cup R^n$ is needed. Warshall's algorithm computes it in $O(n^3)$ bit operations.

items.prompt: Is $R \cup \{(a, c) : (a, b), (b, c) \in R\}$ always the transitive closure of $R$?
items.answer: No. Adding the missing two-step pairs can create new three-step gaps; keep adding (all $R^k$) until no new pairs appear.

items.prompt: An **equivalence relation** is reflexive, {{c1::symmetric}} and {{c2::transitive}}.
items.explanation: "Congruent mod $m$", "same length", "same birthday". A partial order replaces symmetric by antisymmetric.

items.prompt: The equivalence class of $a$ is $[a] = {{c1::\{x : (a, x) \in R\}}}$; and $[a] = [b]$ iff ${{c2::a\,R\,b}}$ iff $[a] \cap [b] \ne \emptyset$.
items.explanation: Two classes are either identical or disjoint; never partially overlapping.

items.prompt: How are equivalence relations and partitions related?
items.answer: The equivalence classes of $R$ form a partition of $A$; conversely every partition defines an equivalence relation ("in the same block"). The correspondence is one-to-one.

items.prompt: What are the equivalence classes of congruence modulo $m$ on $\mathbb{Z}$?
items.answer: $[0], [1], \dots, [m-1]$ with $[r] = \{r + km : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$: exactly $m$ classes, one per remainder.

items.prompt: A **partial ordering** is reflexive, {{c1::antisymmetric}} and {{c2::transitive}}; $(S, \preccurlyeq)$ is then a **poset**.
items.explanation: $(\mathbb{Z}, \le)$, $(\mathbb{Z}^+, \mid)$, $(\mathcal{P}(S), \subseteq)$.

items.prompt: Comparable elements and total order?
items.answer: $a, b$ are comparable if $a \preccurlyeq b$ or $b \preccurlyeq a$. A poset in which every pair is comparable is a total (linear) order, or chain. $(\mathbb{Z}, \le)$ is total; $(\mathbb{Z}^+, \mid)$ is not: $2$ and $3$ are incomparable.

items.prompt: How do you draw the Hasse diagram of a finite poset?
items.answer: Start from the digraph; delete all loops; delete every edge implied by transitivity; arrange so that all remaining edges point upward and drop the arrowheads.

items.prompt: Maximal element vs greatest element of a poset?
items.answer: Maximal: no element is strictly above it (there may be several). Greatest: it is above *every* element (unique if it exists). Greatest implies maximal, not conversely.
items.explanation: Divisibility on $\{2, 3, 4, 6\}$: $4$ and $6$ are maximal, there is no greatest element.

items.prompt: What is a **lattice**?
items.answer: A poset in which every pair of elements has a least upper bound (join) and a greatest lower bound (meet).
items.explanation: $(\mathcal{P}(S), \subseteq)$: join $= \cup$, meet $= \cap$. $(\mathbb{Z}^+, \mid)$: join $= \operatorname{lcm}$, meet $= \gcd$.
